These notes cover only what I could actually read. My research tools ran out before I finished, so several verses (5, 10, 15–21) have little or no material and are left out. Two other gaps: I only saw Enduring Word's summary highlights, not its full commentary, and the Blue Letter Bible copy of Guzik's study guide came back mostly as site navigation. One Catholic article, Jimmy Akin's at catholic.com, I read in full. Points from it have its URL but no quote markers.

## v. 1–2: "Sons of God" and "daughters of men"

**The main views, as traditional teachers set them out**
- Bible.org (Deffinbaugh) says the passage turns on three terms: "sons of God," "daughters of men" and "Nephilim." The interpretation of verses 1-8 hinges upon the definition of three key terms. He describes three views. https://bible.org/seriespage/7-sons-god-and-daughters-men-genesis-61-8
  - **Sethite view:** godly men from Seth's family married ungodly women from Cain's. Its main support is the setting of chapters 4–5. He objects that verse 1 is about mankind in general, so the "daughters" in verse 2 should be general too. (same URL)
  - **Rulers view:** the sons of God were nobles or kings, and their sin was polygamy, like Lamech's. He replies that Israelite kings were never called "sons of God." (same URL)
  - **Fallen-angel view:** this is the one he holds. Fallen angels took on male human form and married women, and the Nephilim were their children. He links this to fallen angels that God now keeps bound. (same URL)
- Don Stewart adds a fourth option: a minority view that sees the distinction between the sons of God and the daughters of men as one simply between men and women, reading 6:1–4 as an epilogue to chapter 5 rather than a lead-in to the Flood. https://www.blueletterbible.org/faq/don_stewart/don_stewart_723.cfm
- David Guzik (Enduring Word / Calvary Chapel) says the Sethite reading leaves open why the sin was bad enough to bring the Flood, and why the children were "unnatural." He notes that "sons of God" clearly refers to angelic creatures when it is used the three other times in the Old Testament (Job 1:6, 2:1, and 38:7). The translators of the Septuagint translated sons of God as "angels." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Gen/Gen-6.cfm
- GotQuestions gives both sides. One article says Peter and Jude seemed to believe the sons of God in Genesis 6:2 were angels who sinned when they stepped outside of their God-given role. https://www.gotquestions.org/sons-of-God-in-Job.html Another raises objections: there is nothing in the text that suggests the "sons of God" are angels. While the phrase can be used of angels…it is also regularly used of people. https://www.gotquestions.org/giants-in-those-days.html

**Where traditions differ**
- **Enduring Word's highlights** suggest Satan may have arranged these demon–human unions to corrupt the human line, so that the Messiah promised in Genesis 3:15 could not be born. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-6/
- **Catholic (Jimmy Akin, Catholic Answers)** rejects the Sethite view. He argues that the phrase "the daughters of men" does not suggest the descendants of Cain. He adds that the unions happened before and after the Flood, which rules out the Sethite view because the line of Cain did not survive the Flood. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/7-mysteries-about-the-nephilim

## v. 3: "My Spirit will not contend… 120 years"

**Traditional reading: 120 years of grace before the Flood**
- Enduring Word: When someone continually rejects God, there is a place of no return where God will no longer strive to persuade that one to repentance and faith. It says the 120 years count down to the Flood, not a limit on lifespan. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-6/
- Keil & Delitzsch: a respite of 120 years should still be granted to the human race. This sentence…was made known to Noah in his 480th year, to be published by him as "preacher of righteousness". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/6-3.htm
- Gill also reads it as time given for repentance, and notes the Targums read it the same way. Barnes says "his days" means the human race, not each person. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/6-3.html
- The NET Bible note (quoted at Precept Austin) says neither the later story nor real life supports reading 120 as a lifespan. It probably means the time left before the Flood. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-6-commentary
- Barnes on "strive": From this passage we learn that the Lord by his Spirit strives with man up to a certain point. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/genesis/6-8.html

**The minority view: a shorter human lifespan**
- Ellicott: the main point of the verse is the Divine determination to shorten human life. https://biblehub.com/genesis/6-3.htm
- Constable notes that Mathews, Westermann and Wenham defend the shorter-life view. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/6-3.html

**Lutheran note**
- Luther, as reported by Don Stewart: Luther translated it I want to give them a reprieve of 120 years. Stewart also says the Hebrew verb behind "strive" is found nowhere else in Scripture and its meaning is uncertain. https://www.blueletterbible.org/faq/don_stewart/don_stewart_730.cfm

**Catholic**
- Haydock (1849) gives both views. He prefers the time-for-repentance reading and says God gave Noah the warning in Noah's 480th year. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/6-3.html
- Akin also prefers a grace period before the Flood. His reasons: no one in Genesis is said to die at 120, and the reading fits 1 Peter 3:20. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/7-mysteries-about-the-nephilim

**Modern scholarship**
- One commentary on the Biblehub page (author not clearly marked) prefers the translation "abide" and lists objections to "strive." It paraphrases the verse as saying that the Spirit God placed in man will not stay in him forever, so mortal life is capped at 120 years. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/6-3.htm

## v. 4: The Nephilim

**Traditional readings**
- **Reformed and Lutheran:** Nephilim means violent men or tyrants. The Pulpit Commentary prefers men of violence, roving, lawless gallants, "who fall on others;" robbers, or tyrants (Aquila, Rosenmüller, Gesenius, Luther, Calvin, Kurtz, Keil. Keil adds: Luther gives the correct meaning, "tyrants:" they were called Nephilim because they fell upon the people and oppressed them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/6-4.htm
- Keil argues the grammar shows the Nephilim were already on earth before these marriages. If so, they give no evidence that the sons of God were angels. (same URL)
- Calvin, on "men of renown": "the first nobility of the world, honorable robbers, who boasted of their wickedness". (same URL)
- **Fallen-angel view:** Guzik says these giants were unique because of the demonic element of their parentage. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Gen/Gen-6.cfm
- **GotQuestions** is cautious: The passage does not explicitly say how these giants came to be. It suggests that after the Flood "Nephilim" had become a semi-technical term for "giant warrior." https://www.gotquestions.org/Nephilim.html ; https://www.gotquestions.org/Goliath-Nephilim.html

**"And afterward as well"**
- One older commentary on Biblehub says these words were very probably added as a gloss, in order to shew that the Nephilim existed not only in primitive ages, but also at the time of the Exodus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/6-4.htm
- Catholic (Akin): The Nephilim were on the earth both before and after the Flood because the sons of God and the daughters of men mated twice. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/7-mysteries-about-the-nephilim

**Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey)**
- Calls 6:1–4 a famously difficult passage that tells of an apparent breach in the boundary between the divine and the human realms. It says the Nephilim's origins remain notoriously vague. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/nephilim/
- It explains that in 1 Enoch the sons of God are rebel angels called Watchers, whose children were monstrous giants. (same URL)

**Popular teaching**
- GotQuestions answers popular claims directly: The Nephilim were not aliens, angels, "Watchers," or rock monsters; they were literal, physical beings. https://www.gotquestions.org/Nephilim.html

## v. 5: Human wickedness
- GotQuestions links the Nephilim to the growing evil of verse 5 and the violence of verses 11 and 13. It suggests the "mighty men" and "heroes of old" may have strong-armed others into submission. Their violent oppression is part of what led to the flood. https://www.gotquestions.org/heroes-of-old.html

---

## v. 6–7: God "regretted" and was grieved
- Bible.org (Deffinbaugh) starts from God's unchanging nature (Numbers 23:19). He says "God repented" is an anthropomorphism, meaning human language used to describe God. https://bible.org/seriespage/7-sons-god-and-daughters-men-genesis-61-8
- He goes on: While God's will (His decree) cannot and does not change, He is free to change His emotions. Grief is love's response to sin. God is no stoic. (same URL)

## v. 8: "Noah found favor"
- Ellicott: This is the first place where grace is mentioned in the Bible. https://biblehub.com/genesis/6-8.htm
- Barnes: Now for the first time grace itself finds a tongue to express its name. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/6-8.html
- Matthew Henry: Noah was probably hated by people because his life and preaching condemned the world, but he found grace with God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/6-8.htm

**Where traditions differ: why Noah found grace**
- **Reformed (Calvin):** he warns against those who think people find grace through their own effort and merit. He grants that Noah lived uprightly, but asks where that integrity came from but from the preventing grace of God? https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/6-8.html
- **Reformed Baptist (Gill):** this was owing to the grace of God, and his choice upon that, and not to the merits of the creature. He also calls Noah's family a remnant "according to the election of grace." (same URL)
- **Methodist (Benson):** Noah was by nature corrupt and sinful, he had been renewed in the spirit of his mind, and by repentance and a lively faith, had obtained witness that he was righteous. Note the Wesleyan stress on renewal and the "witness" of being accepted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/6-8.htm
- **Restoration Movement (sermon outline at CCEL):** lists reasons Noah found grace: he was just, blameless, walked with God, obeyed and preached righteousness. It applies this to baptism through 1 Peter 3:20–21. https://www.ccel.org/contrib/exec_outlines/text/gen6_8.htm
- **Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel):** Noah found favor in the sight of the Lord because He had faith in the word of the Lord. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_chuck/SermonNotes_Gen/Gen_18.cfm

## v. 9: "Righteous… blameless… walked with God"
- CCEL outline: "blameless" does not mean sinless, but that he had no blatant faults…He was a man of moral integrity among the people. In walking with God he followed the example of Enoch. https://www.ccel.org/contrib/exec_outlines/text/gen6_8.htm
- Clarke: a "just man" is a man who gave to all their due. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cev/genesis/6-8.html
- **A disputed reading:** Enduring Word's highlights say "perfect in his generations" means not only Noah's character but his genetic purity. On that view, he alone was untouched by Satan's attempt to corrupt the human line. This depends on the fallen-angel reading of verse 2. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-6/

---

## v. 11–13: Corruption and violence
- A homily on Biblehub sees two marks of the general turning away from God: The first is moral corruption; the second, violence. It adds: To walk with God is the true way to make men gentle and pitying. https://biblehub.com/sermons/genesis/6-8.htm

---

## v. 14: Gopher wood, rooms, pitch
- Ellicott: "gopher" occurs only here but probably means cypress. "Rooms" literally means "nests," and "pitch" is natural bitumen. He says the account reads like the work of people living inland, unlike the Babylonian flood story. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/6-14.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: once hardened, the pitch would make it perfectly watertight. (same URL)
- Coffman: The ark was not designed to sail, but merely to float. Calvin says there is no reason to worry over the details of its structure, except as far as they help us. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/6-14.html
- Matthew Henry: pitch outside kept the water out, pitch inside kept down the animals' smell. Observe, God does not bid him paint it, but pitch it. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/genesis/6-14.html
- Word note: the verb "pitch" (kaphar) means "to cover," and figuratively "to expiate." The noun (kopher) can figuratively mean "a redemption-price." https://biblehub.com/lexicon/genesis/6-14.htm
- **The ark as a picture of Christ (Reformed, Ligonier):** the ark foreshadows salvation from sin and death (1 Peter 3:18–22). Ligonier compares its size to a modern battleship and says the identity of gopher wood is unknown. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ark-gopher-wood
- Biblical Illustrator: the ark is God's appointed way of safety and a test of faith. It makes the point that taking refuge in Christ is more than knowing he is the Deliverer. https://biblehub.com/sermons/genesis/6-14.htm

---

## v. 22: Noah's obedience
- Enduring Word's highlights: Noah carried out a huge 120-year building project without complaint and preached righteousness. Apparently no one else believed him and entered the ark. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-6/
- CCEL outline: the obedience is stressed twice (6:22; 7:5), and Hebrews 11:7 shows it came from faith. https://www.ccel.org/contrib/exec_outlines/text/gen6_8.htm
- Precept Austin: He worked because he had faith (see James 2:17). https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-6-commentary
